sections.text: Rust’s traits are a single concept that unifies interfaces, abstract classes, mix-ins, operator overloading, contraints on generics, and more.

Keeping cache work bounded without hiding what readers lose when telemetry updates are discarded or arrive late. I wanted to update a cache as device readings passed through an existing telemetry pipeline. The processor would still publish its events; the cache would keep the latest readings ready for queries. A slow cache, however, would leave the processor with updates waiting to be written. I needed a limit on that work and a decision about what to lose when the limit was reached. The design keeps a bounded set of pending updates, allowing a newer reading to replace an older one for the same device and metric. Revisiting the implementation showed how much depends on what happens after that replacement: which value a writer receives, which write finishes last, and whether a lost reading ever gets another chance. For a device that stops reporting, a dropped final reading may leave the person using the view with a gap that later traffic from other devices cannot repair. 1 When a consumer cannot keep up 1.1 A queue buys time 1.2 Where the pressure goes 2 A bounded write path for current readings 2.1 Coalesce by device and metric 2.2 Writers must consume the state being coalesced 2.3 Bound everything that retains work 2.4 Preserve ordering at the final write 2.5 A dropped final update does not repair itself 2.6 What I give up, and where the design stops working 3 How I would evolve the system 3.1 Start with the freshness readers need 3.2 Give repair a budget 3.3 Scale the constrained part

sections.heading: 1 When a consumer cannot keep up
sections.text: In From Time-Series to State, I described keeping the latest known device readings in a cache so that queries would not have to reconstruct them from history. That moves work from readers to the ingestion path. Now a processor that already enriches and publishes events also has to maintain the cache. I did not want cache writes to hold up event publication. Pranshu Raj's Backpressure in Distributed Systems discusses the choices available when producers outpace consumers, including slowing producers and dropping work. The cache gives me room to discard some updates; the event log has a different delivery requirement.

sections.heading: 1.1 A queue buys time
sections.text: Suppose a consumer completes 80 updates per second while 100 arrive. With room for 200 updates, an empty queue fills in about ten seconds. These illustrative numbers assume constant rates and equal-cost updates: capacity divided by the excess arrival rate gives us the time until the queue fills. A larger queue absorbs a longer burst. If overload continues, it also makes accepted work wait longer before the queue fills anyway. Launching a goroutine for each blocked send leaves the waiting events in memory, now attached to goroutines. To stay within a memory budget, the system eventually has to accept less work, complete it faster, or discard some of it.

sections.heading: 1.2 Where the pressure goes
sections.text: I use backpressure for feedback that limits what an upstream stage submits. A blocking channel can provide that feedback locally. An asynchronous consumer can advertise demand or stop requesting more work, as in the Reactive Streams model. The submitting thread need not block for the flow of work to slow down. Rejecting an update without slowing its producer is load shedding. Replacing several pending updates with one is coalescing. These protect the consumer without necessarily changing the arrival rate. My cache design relies on both, so calling the whole mechanism backpressure would leave out an important part of its behavior: ingestion can continue while cache updates are lost. When required event processing slows down, a durable log can retain the backlog. Lag still grows, downstream views become stale, and retention is finite. The cache is an optional projection, so I can discard work there to preserve capacity for publication. I can make that trade-off because a newer temperature observation supersedes an older one in the current-state view. It would be wrong for an increment in a consumption total or for an alarm transition or billing event: losing one could change the answer. Even when coalescing is appropriate for a view, historical events may still need to be retained elsewhere.

sections.heading: 2 A bounded write path for current readings
sections.text: My proposal gives the processor a secondary, best-effort path to the current-state cache. It offers each processed measurement to a bounded buffer and continues without waiting for cache I/O. Writers take work from the buffer in batches. If they fall behind, pending updates can be discarded while publication continues. Both paths still share the processor's CPU and memory. The cache branch needs a resource budget even though it does not wait for I/O on the primary path. Figure 1: The intended separation of responsibilities. Cache admission may coalesce or shed updates; required publication needs its own bounded, acknowledged path. The cache branch is a design, not a guarantee of delivery.

sections.heading: 2.1 Coalesce by device and metric
sections.text: A device reports different metrics independently. Replacing a pending temperature update must not remove its pending voltage reading, so the queue's identity is the pair (device, metric). The proposed ring buffer has a fixed number of slots and an index mapping each identity to its slot. A newer observation for an existing identity replaces the pending value in place. An older observation is ignored. When a new identity arrives at capacity, the queue evicts its oldest pending entry. Consider a queue with these pending entries: Device Metric Observation time Value A temperature 10:00:00 21.4 C A voltage 10:00:01 3.5 V B temperature 10:00:02 19.8 C If A/temperature arrives with time 10:00:03, it replaces the first value. The queue still has three pending identities, and the writer can skip the superseded temperature reading. The index avoids scanning for it: lookups are expected O(1), while ring insertion and eviction are O(1). In-place replacement leaves the slot where it was. "Oldest" then means the earliest admitted pending identity, even if its value has just changed. Moving every replacement to the back would change how frequently reporting metrics are evicted. Either policy is possible, but they give different results.

sections.heading: 2.2 Writers must consume the state being coalesced
sections.text: Revisiting the implementation exposed a gap in this design. It keeps recent observations in a ring and sends copies to a separate bounded channel. Writers receive those copies. Replacing a ring entry leaves an older copy already in the channel untouched. If the channel rejects the newer copy, nothing arranges another attempt to deliver the value still held in the ring. Suppose the device stops reporting at that point. The ring holds its newest reading, but the writer may never see it. The ring is acting as a recent-value registry with best-effort notifications, while the proposal needs it to be the queue of pending work. I would have writers claim entries directly from that queue. A channel can wake a writer when work arrives without carrying another set of event copies. The following pseudocode sketches the change; these operations would still need to be implemented: Admission and claiming share one synchronization boundary; network writes happen outside it. offer(event): # while holding the queue lock reject if admission is closed key = (event.device, event.metric) if key is pending: replace only if event.version is newer else: evict oldest pending entry if at capacity insert key and event signal work available claim_batch(limit): # while holding the same lock remove up to limit pending entries remove their index entries return immutable snapshots for the writer Once a writer claims an entry, a newer observation for that metric can become pending again while the earlier write is in flight. If that write fails, its cleanup must leave the newer pending entry alone. Wake-ups may be combined, provided a worker checks the queue before sleeping and cannot miss the transition from empty to nonempty. Admission can briefly wait for the lock protecting the ring and index. "Nonblocking" here means that it does not wait for queue capacity or cache I/O. The writer also needs to copy the claimed event under that lock, before another producer can change its contents. Figure 2: Proposed admission and writer control flow. The queue and index share a mutex; cache writes happen after claiming and unlocking. Slow writes reduce the drain rate, so admission eventually evicts pending work rather than waiting for cache capacity. This is bounded overload control, not producer throttling. The version policy shown ignores older and equal versions; corrections need the ordering policy discussed below.

sections.heading: 2.3 Bound everything that retains work
sections.text: The ring's fixed capacity limits its entry count. To estimate memory, I also have to account for the values themselves and everything else that retains them: the index, worker mailboxes and batches, encoding buffers, and cache clients. Variable-sized values need a size limit or a byte budget before I can claim a memory bound. In the proposed single-pending-queue design, a rough payload allowance is (C + W * B) * Emax: pending capacity C, W workers, at most B claimed events per worker, and maximum retained event size Emax. Index and client overhead need their own allowances. The existing implementation also has copies and extra channels, so this expression does not bound its memory usage. A small worker pool limits simultaneous application-level writes if each worker waits for its write to finish. Counting client objects gives no such assurance, since a client may manage several connections. And without write deadlines, a stalled cache can leave every worker occupied indefinitely. Batch size and the flush deadline let me trade waiting time for less network overhead. Here too, the implementation needs a closer look: the writer collects a batch, but the storage adapter executes its pipeline separately for each event. Changing the batch size will not give it one network execution per batch.

sections.heading: 2.4 Preserve ordering at the final write
sections.text: A writer can claim a temperature reading just before a newer one arrives. Another writer may claim the newer reading and finish first. If both writes are unconditional, the older reading then overwrites it. Coalescing while observations are pending does not protect them once they are in flight. The current dispatcher assigns work round-robin, so updates for a key can reach different workers even if they arrived in partition order. Its cache writes are unconditional. The registry's timestamp comparison cannot prevent this later overwrite. The cache needs to apply the same rule: replace a metric only when the incoming version is newer. With concurrent writers, comparison and replacement must be atomic. Reading the version in a client and then writing leaves room for another writer to act between the two operations. A cache-side conditional update can close that race. Exclusive ownership of a key is another option, provided it covers every writer, including recovery. Choosing a version also commits us to an ordering policy. Observation timestamps depend on the devices' clocks and reset behavior; equal timestamps, corrections, and sequence resets need explicit handling. Arrival order will not resolve this when replay or delayed delivery can reorder observations.

sections.heading: 2.5 A dropped final update does not repair itself
sections.text: I left retries out of the initial proposal because a later reading could replace a lost one. For a frequently reporting metric, that may be an acceptable delay. But it assumes that another reading arrives and its write succeeds. If the device goes offline instead, its last update may remain missing. That is where my original claim of eventual consistency needs qualification. To promise eventual recovery of that observation, the system needs replay or reconciliation. Historical storage can supply the data; something still has to find the missing state and repair it. I also need to know where loss occurs. Ignoring an older observation discards superseded work. Evicting a pending entry or failing a write can lose a value the cache needs. The current path counts outcomes at one boundary, while dispatch can drop silently and the worker discards the returned write error. A single "dropped" counter would hide the distinction even if it counted all of these cases. Meanwhile, event publication remains a separate responsibility. It is not transactional with cache admission: a cache update can succeed even when publication fails. Launching an unbounded goroutine for each publication would also defeat the memory budget. The required path needs its own publication acknowledgement and input-offset handling.

sections.heading: 2.6 What I give up, and where the design stops working
sections.text: The appeal of this design is that cache trouble does not force the processor to retain an ever-growing backlog. Coalescing removes superseded work, while eviction gives the queue a way to stay within capacity. I pay for that with incomplete state and potentially longer delays before a device's next reading reaches the cache. Avoiding retries keeps the write path simple, but leaves recovery to later observations or a separate repair mechanism. A process that stays alive through overload has met only part of the requirement. Its cache can still be too stale to use.

sections.heading: 2.6.1 When there is little work to coalesce
sections.text: Repeated temperature updates for one device are cheap to hold: they share one pending slot. The same number of updates spread over different devices and metrics may each need a slot and a write. Event rate alone therefore says little about how much this design saves. If the writes required to keep those metrics within the chosen freshness target exceed the cache's sustained capacity, no finite buffer can meet that target indefinitely. A larger ring buys time during a burst. Under sustained overload, it can retain more work while the view continues to fall behind. Shedding may keep the service running, but it cannot preserve the promised freshness and coverage at the same time. The eviction policy also makes no promise to each device. Enough new identities can displace a rarely reporting metric before a writer claims it. If its device then stays quiet, frequent updates elsewhere do nothing to repair that missing value. A single hot key cannot fill this deduplicating queue on its own; competition comes from the number of different keys needing service. There are two memory limits to consider as well. The pending queue must fit in the processor, and the retained current-state dataset must fit in the cache. Bounding the queue does not bound the number of devices and metrics stored over time. If that dataset exceeds available cache memory, capacity or retention has to change. Otherwise writes can fail or stored entries may be evicted, depending on the cache policy, independently of the pending queue's behavior.

sections.heading: 2.6.2 When best effort becomes a broken promise
sections.text: This design is a poor fit when every observation matters, or when every device must appear in the view within a fixed deadline despite failures. Eviction and unretried write failures explicitly allow those requirements to be violated. A larger buffer cannot change the delivery contract. Even for a current-state view, accepting occasional loss is a stronger choice for a metric that reports rarely than for one that reports frequently. I would need repair if the last reading before a device goes offline must eventually appear. If the source no longer retains that observation, or no recovery path can read it, the cache cannot reconstruct it. Version checks depend on trustworthy ordering too. With timestamps as versions, one erroneous future timestamp can cause subsequent normal readings to be rejected until they overtake it. Atomic comparison would faithfully enforce the wrong order. Clock validation or a suitable version and correction policy has to resolve that; coalescing cannot.

sections.heading: 2.6.3 When cache trouble spreads to the primary path
sections.text: The secondary path shares a process with required publication. It still spends CPU on each offered event, takes the queue lock, and allocates or encodes data. A bounded queue limits retained work, not the cost of an unlimited stream of admission attempts. If that work exhausts shared CPU or creates enough memory pressure, publication can slow down even though admission never waits for cache capacity. Fixed workers and byte limits reduce the risk; separate resource budgets, and eventually process isolation, may be needed for a stronger boundary. Recovery can spread the load in the other direction. If cache misses make readers query history, an outage can move the read workload onto the historical store. If replay then competes with live writes at full speed, recovery can overload the cache again. Google's Addressing Cascading Failures describes how shifting load after a failure can exhaust the remaining capacity. Fallback and repair need admission limits of their own. Repair given only spare capacity will never catch up while live work consumes the entire write budget. I would use this approach for a replaceable current-state projection whose readers tolerate visible gaps or delay, with enough normal capacity to recover after bursts. If the requirement becomes complete, deadline-bound delivery for every metric, I would need durable pending work or replay, flow control, and capacity sized for that requirement. The bounded ring would still be useful as a local optimization, but it would no longer be the delivery mechanism.

sections.heading: 3 How I would evolve the system
sections.text: Once the cache branch stays within its resource budget, I still need to agree with the people using the view how stale or incomplete it may become. They need to recognize when it is behind, and the people operating it need a recovery path they can manage. Those requirements guide what I would change next.

sections.heading: 3.1 Start with the freshness readers need
sections.text: Queue occupancy alone would tell me too little. I would also track the oldest pending work, the delay until a successful write, and the reasons updates are lost. Observation age needs separate attention: a quiet device can have an old reading while ingestion is healthy. Broker lag helps distinguish that case from a processor that has fallen behind. A queue full of repeated updates for a few metrics is a good candidate for coalescing. If most entries belong to different metrics, that will buy less; admission or capacity needs to change. Slow writes while little work is pending call for a different investigation again. A larger queue can make the screen staler without speeding up any of those writes. I would measure retained bytes and write cost alongside events per second. Google's Handling Overload discusses the limits of request-count capacity models and the value of treating work differently according to its criticality. Here, required publication and a replaceable cache projection already have different delivery requirements.

sections.heading: 3.2 Give repair a budget
sections.text: After bounding the write path and enforcing ordering, I would add a repair path that can identify stale or missing state and recover it from the source. Recovery needs a rate limit too. Replaying everything at full speed after an outage can overload the cache just as it becomes available again. Live updates and repair could share a write budget, with repair using spare capacity. The version rule must apply to both, so a delayed historical read cannot overwrite a newer observation. When the freshness target cannot be met within that budget, the service should report that the view is degraded. A normal shutdown can leave missing work as well. I would stop admission and join the producers, then drain accepted work within a deadline before closing the clients. Anything left needs to be counted and covered by repair. A fixed sleep cannot tell me whether the writers have finished.

sections.heading: 3.3 Scale the constrained part
sections.text: More workers can help while the cache has spare write capacity. Beyond that, they increase contention or move the wait into connection pools. Partitioning the pending queue would bring ownership and rebalancing into the ordering design. If a noisy source repeatedly crowds out rarely reporting devices, separate allowances may be needed to protect their pending updates. I would wait for evidence of those problems before adding the machinery. The delivery and ordering gaps need fixing first; tuning an adaptive concurrency controller would be difficult while write errors and missing updates were still indistinguishable. I would test this with the cache unavailable, checking that publication continues within its own admission limits and pending cache work stays bounded. During recovery, readers must still be able to tell when their view is behind, while repair catches up without displacing live traffic. Until that behavior is established, I would describe the projection as best effort rather than promise eventual consistency.

documents.title: Backpressure in a Telemetry Pipeline: What Happens When the Cache Falls Behind?

sections.text: Why an accepted write can still leave a dashboard behind, explored through a small journal design in Go and Rust. A client submits a device event. The service replies accepted. An operator refreshes the dashboard and still sees the old value. The event may already be safely recorded. The table behind the dashboard is still catching up. Without some indication of its progress, the operator has no way to tell a delayed view from a missing update. Decide what “accepted” means Choose who pays for the lookup Pay when somebody reads Pay before replying Pay after replying Put freshness in the answer Give unfinished work a budget Decide who owns the batch What changes at the handoff Look at the allocation pattern Ask whether the same work is necessary Change which bytes move Spend memory and maintenance where they help Schedule maintenance with foreground demand Measure acknowledgement and visibility What the local runs showed Choose the language at the constraint that matters References Recording an event and making it available to readers can finish at different times. The service needs to say which of those it has promised when it replies. Updating the table before replying closes this visibility gap for readers of that table. Moving the update into a worker can shorten the acknowledgement path, provided the service tracks the work still waiting. If lookups are rare, it may be cheaper to scan the journal when a query arrives and maintain no table at all. I want to compare those choices through a small journal design in Go and Rust. The interesting question is where the lookup work belongs, and what a fast acknowledgement leaves the service to finish afterward. The code also gives us a concrete place to compare the languages' ownership and synchronization rules. Choose who pays for the lookup
sections.text: The three policies append the same records. They differ in when they do the work needed by readers. Figure 1: Three dependency paths for the same journal records. Background acknowledgement and replay branch after publication. Admission may still delay the next append. Arrows show dependencies, not durations. Open the full-size diagram

sections.heading: Pay when somebody reads
sections.text: With no lookup table, a query can scan backward in blocks from a captured journal boundary. It stops at the first record for the device. A recent value may be quick to find; a device with no record requires scanning the entire captured history. This avoids maintaining a table for events nobody queries. It becomes expensive when an investigation asks for many old values or missing devices. Infrequent reads can still have a response-time requirement.

sections.heading: Pay before replying
sections.text: The eager writer updates the in-memory table after synchronization and before replying. A subsequent reader of that same table, using the same lock, can see the write or a later update. A different replica or response cache needs its own visibility guarantee. The table can remain in memory because the journal is enough to rebuild it. Persisting the table would be a separate choice to reduce recovery time. For a small table, updating it directly may cost less than coordinating a worker.

sections.heading: Pay after replying
sections.text: A background worker replays the published journal prefix into the table. The writer can usually reply without waiting for that replay. The service does, however, pay for another read pass, decoding and checksum verification, as well as worker coordination. Those reads may hit the page cache and avoid physical I/O, but still use CPU and memory bandwidth. Moving replay out of the acknowledgement path can shorten the response while increasing total work. For a service with rare lookups, a scan may be enough. Frequent reads can justify a table. A worker is worth adding when the shorter acknowledgement path is useful enough to pay for replay and delayed visibility.

sections.heading: Put freshness in the answer
Give unfinished work a budget
Decide who owns the batch
What changes at the handoff
Look at the allocation pattern
Ask whether the same work is necessary
sections.text: Moving work to a different thread is only one way to change the trade-off. Storage research also changes the representation, memory allocation, and amount of maintenance required. The RUM conjecture describes a trade-off between read cost, update cost, and memory or storage overhead: optimizing two tends to come at the expense of the third. It is a conjecture about access methods, not a rule that fixes the best design for this service. For our projection, it is a reason to include space in the comparison alongside read and write costs. Freshness and backlog are additional service constraints.

sections.heading: Change which bytes move
sections.text: WiscKey (FAST 2016) keeps keys and value locations in an LSM-tree while storing values in a separate log. This reduces value movement during compaction, at the cost of managing that log and changing range-query access patterns. It suggests a useful question for our worker: how much of each event actually needs to be copied, decoded, or reorganized?

sections.heading: Spend memory and maintenance where they help
sections.text: Monkey (SIGMOD 2017) distributes Bloom-filter memory across LSM levels to reduce the combined false-positive cost of lookups. Giving every level the same bits per key misses that opportunity. Dostoevsky (SIGMOD 2018) reduces merging where it contributes little to point lookups, long range queries, or space reclamation. Its design also accounts for the different needs of short range queries. That distinction matters when deciding which maintenance work earns its cost. For the journal, the corresponding question is which representation earns its maintenance cost under the queries people actually make.

sections.heading: Schedule maintenance with foreground demand
sections.text: EcoTune (SIGMOD 2025) treats compaction as an investment of CPU and I/O resources to improve future queries. HATS (FAST 2026), implemented in Cassandra, combines replica selection for reads with adaptive compaction rate control.,  Neither paper implements this projection protocol. They address a problem the worker shares with compaction: background tasks compete with foreground requests for the resources intended to make those requests faster. A writer can slow down even when it never waits directly for the worker. Both still use the same CPU, caches, memory bandwidth, and storage device. For the journal, this leaves several choices worth measuring: reduce the bytes replayed, maintain less state, or schedule replay around foreground demand. Changing threads is only one option.

sections.heading: Measure acknowledgement and visibility
sections.text: The producer needs an acknowledgement. The operator needs a sufficiently fresh answer. The service must sustain both without accumulating an ever-growing backlog. Whose requirement? Measure What a misleading result leaves out Producer Arrival-to-acknowledgement latency Upstream queueing and batch formation Operator Visibility delay and lookup latency at a stated freshness Whether the answer includes the write Service Lag, catch-up time, CPU, memory, and physical I/O Work still unfinished when the timer stops Recovery Time to the required serving state Which representations must actually be rebuilt The companion records batch acknowledgement timing, time in the lag gate, maximum record lag, and catch-up time after writes stop. Its lookups run over the same completed history in all three designs. The gate timer includes acquiring and checking the mutex even when no wait is needed, so it is not a pure blocked-time measure. Those post-drain lookups still leave the operator's experience untested. To measure live freshness and interference, queries must run while writes continue. A timer around a ready batch also excludes upstream queueing and time spent waiting for the batch to fill. The companion uses the same 32-byte record format, deterministic input, batching, table layout, worker batch size, and lag limit in both languages. An independently generated fixture checks the encoder, and the comparison runner checks journal hashes and query results. Buffered writes belong in a separate comparison from synchronized writes because their acknowledgement contracts differ. The harness does not collect process CPU, RSS, allocation profiles, or physical device I/O. Its read-byte counters include data served from the page cache, and its table-size counter covers only logical entry payload. A sustained experiment needs those additional measurements and must run long enough for a slow worker to reach its lag limit. A short run with writes followed by catch-up cannot establish a service-level latency or freshness guarantee. Measure recovery to the serving state each policy actually requires. A journal-only service need not build a projection before answering queries. A projection-backed service may choose to finish replay before serving or expose partial progress. Recovering from a partial trailing record also needs testing separately from broader power-loss behavior.

sections.heading: What the local runs showed
sections.text: The measurements below were run locally on this machine: Component Configuration Processor Apple M3 Max, 16 CPU cores, arm64 (Mac15,9) Memory 128 GiB Operating system macOS 26.6.2, build 25G83 Storage Internal storage, APFS filesystem Toolchains Go 1.27.3 and Rust 1.99.1, optimized builds Runtime settings AC power; GOMAXPROCS=16; no CPU affinity or quota Runs used normal filesystem caching, without cache eviction or exclusive machine access. Each condition ran seven times in randomized order, with one benchmark process at a time. All 168 measured runs agreed on journal bytes and query results within their workloads; twelve warmup runs were excluded. These results describe this machine and workload, rather than a hardware-independent performance expectation. For the synchronized baseline, 100,000 records in batches of 64 took roughly seven seconds under each policy. The background worker showed no consistent acknowledgement advantage, and every synchronized background run peaked at just one batch of lag. Synchronization made this a poor workload for testing pressure on a 4,096-record budget. The longer buffered runs made the maintenance cost easier to see. Each wrote two million records across 4,096 possible keys. The table held only 64 KiB of logical entry data. These are medians of seven runs; the p99 columns summarize the seven per-run batch percentiles. M3 Max, 16 cores, 128 GiB RAM, macOS 26.6.2, APFS. Vertical offsets separate overlapping points and have no data meaning. Buffered writes only; queries and recovery are outside the timed phase. Open the full-size plot Here, the background median elapsed time was about 40% higher than eager maintenance in both implementations. Its batch-acknowledgement p99 was higher too. Updating this small table directly was cheap; the worker added replay and coordination, including another logical read of all 64 MB of journal data. Moving that work into a worker did not pay off in this experiment. These buffered numbers do not describe synchronized-write throughput. Reducing both the lag limit and worker block to 64 records exercised tighter coordination. All fourteen background runs reached that bound without exceeding it. Median write-and-drain time rose to 206.73 ms in Go and 313.19 ms in Rust. Because both settings changed, and the unchanged eager controls also ran faster in this later campaign, I would not attribute an exact slowdown to the lag limit alone. The journal-only policy paid at query time: post-drain lookup p99 medians were about 28 ms in Go and 20 ms in Rust in the longer buffered workload, which included 36 absent-device queries out of 256. Table lookups were close to the timer's resolution. Those measurements show why the read workload matters; they do not predict HTTP latency or settle a language choice. A larger or more expensive projection could change the maintenance comparison, but this experiment has not demonstrated that benefit.

sections.heading: Choose the language at the constraint that matters
sections.text: For an existing Go ingestion service with adequate memory headroom and contained ownership boundaries, Go is a reasonable starting point. For a new storage component dominated by buffer recycling, reclamation, and shared mutable state, Rust's static ownership constraints can be a substantial advantage. Profiling should precede a rewrite. If synchronization accounts for an assumed 90% of operation time and stays unchanged, halving everything else reduces total time by 5%, equivalent to about a 1.053× speedup. That arithmetic does not predict either language's result. The Go worker runs in a goroutine; the Rust worker uses a dedicated standard-library thread. They have different scheduling models. These examples do not compare async runtimes. Both programs stop and join their worker on normal completion and returned errors. Go defers the stop-and-wait procedure before file cleanup. Rust performs it explicitly before propagating the write result; dropping a join handle alone would detach the thread. The full Rust worker also catches unwinding panics and explicitly publishes failure to wake waiters. That does not make shutdown generally panic-safe: the excerpts still panic on a poisoned mutex, and an abort or permanently blocked I/O operation lies outside that mechanism. Poisoning itself is advisory and does not establish whether the state is intact.,  For the operator refreshing the dashboard, the useful response is a value with a stated progress position, or a clear timeout waiting for the requested write. For the service, that promise has a cost: once replay falls far enough behind, new writes must wait or be rejected. I would establish that behavior under a mixed workload before using acknowledgement latency to choose an indexing policy or a language. The companion contains both journal implementations, an independent byte fixture, tests, and a comparison runner. The separate handoff examples illustrate buffer ownership; they are not another journal policy. Article excerpts omit setup and instrumentation and are not standalone programs. Checks passed with the project's pinned Go 1.27.3 and Rust 1.99.1 toolchains on macOS/arm64: nine core Go tests and two handoff tests with the race detector, vet for both Go packages, five core Rust tests and three handoff tests in debug and release, and the ownership compile-fail doctest in both profiles. Optimized binaries completed 168 measured runs with matching journal hashes and query checksums within each workload. Every measured background run stayed within its lag limit. The measurements use one writer, fixed-size records, a small dense table, and queries only after catch-up. They are local comparisons, not a production capacity estimate or a general performance ranking of Go and Rust. Concurrent live freshness, process-resource use, physical device I/O, and power-loss behavior remain unqualified.

How Rust's Iterator trait supports lazy composition, and what a comparison with C++ ranges tells us about ownership checks and optimization. I can read a chain of enumerate(), filter(), and take() and understand what it asks for. I find it harder to picture what is actually running. Does each step traverse the data again? What does the chain borrow, and what work stops when we stop asking for values? We'll build a small adapter, extend the pattern to prefix sums, and follow a query over borrowed telemetry records. The aim is to understand how the Iterator contract lets these pieces compose, and how ownership and dispatch affect the code we can write. That also gives us a basis for deciding when an ordinary iterator is enough and when asynchronous streams or coroutines help. C++ ranges provide a useful comparison because they support lazy composition too. Looking at both languages helps distinguish the techniques they share from Rust's compile-time checks on borrowing. This gives us a way to judge the safety and potential costs of an iterator-based design, including which performance claims still need measurement. sections.text: A path through the notebook’s Org publishing examples: inspect what survives export, see it in a working article, and distinguish stored results from live execution. A note in Emacs and a page on the web serve different purposes. The useful question is not whether they look identical, but whether the structure, examples, and connections that make the note useful survive the journey. This guide connects two working examples in the notebook. Start with the publishing fixture to inspect individual features, then read the Rust article to see those features supporting an explanation. Inspect the publishing surface Read an example in context Keep the connections in the source Read another author’s workflow Questions to explore next

sections.heading: Inspect the publishing surface
sections.text: The Org-mode publishing showcase deliberately puts headings, tables, task states, inline formatting, and source blocks together. It is the place to look when asking a narrow question: does this part of an Org document still make sense after export? The route here is Org → ox-hugo Markdown → Berlin’s semantic document → HTML. Each stage has a different responsibility. Emacs remains the authoring environment; the published page does not reproduce folding, agendas, or capture workflows. The showcase documents examples, not a promise of support for every Org feature.

sections.heading: Read an example in context
sections.text: Processing JSON with Rust is a learning exercise rather than a publishing test. Read it for the relationship between the prose, the source listings, and the medal results. Code references let an explanation point to a precise part of a listing without turning the whole article into a wall of code. The worked medal pipeline also makes a useful distinction visible: showing the steps of an execution is not the same as executing a program in the reader’s browser. Stored Org results can accompany source code; Berlin’s publishing export does not execute the code blocks again.

sections.heading: Keep the connections in the source
sections.text: The links above are Org ID links. Their targets are document identities, not hand-maintained HTML filenames. Berlin resolves them against the published collection and derives backlinks to the passages that refer to each note. That division keeps two different kinds of organisation separate. Tags gather material with shared labels. A guide chooses a route through that material and explains why each stop belongs. The explanation remains ordinary prose, so it can change as the notebook grows.

sections.heading: Read another author’s workflow
sections.text: Dominik Honnef’s My org-roam workflows for taking notes and writing articles describes a broader system connecting notes, references, and web publication. His use of category notes is especially relevant here: a category can contain an explanation as well as collect links. It offers a useful comparison, not a description of the configuration used by this website.

sections.heading: Questions to explore next
sections.text: These two questions are starting points for further investigation, not completed experiments. Each connects something already in the notebook to a small next step.

sections.heading: What would make a stored result reproducible?
sections.text: The worked example in Processing JSON with Rust places a small input beside its extraction, counting, and ranking results. That makes the explanation inspectable. It does not, by itself, establish that another environment will produce the same result. The uncertainty is what needs to accompany the stored output: the exact input, source listings, dependency lockfile, Rust toolchain, and execution command are a starting point. Is that enough to reproduce this particular example? A small experiment would be to use a disposable copy of the example, record those inputs, and compare a fresh execution with the stored table. Then change one medal in the small input and regenerate the results. Record what changed and whether the explanation still matches. Run this explicitly during authoring; the publishing export should continue to use stored results. The useful follow-up would be a short note containing the recorded setup, comparison, and any mismatch—not a claim of reproducibility before trying it.

sections.heading: Where should a guide end and a note begin?
sections.text: This guide introduces both the publishing showcase and the Rust learning exercise. The uncertainty is how much orientation belongs here without repeating the explanations in those notes. A small reading exercise would be to follow the links with two different questions: “Which Org features can I inspect?” and “How do code references support an explanation?” For each route, record the first place where context is missing or unnecessarily repeated. Put route-finding context in the guide and keep the technical explanation beside its example. The result may be only a revised paragraph or a better link. A separate note is useful when there is an observation worth explaining, not just to fill out the collection.

Serving current device readings without reconstructing them from history, while keeping the age of each observation visible. A table of device readings was slow during ordinary use. Someone opening it had to wait while the backend looked up the latest observations, assembled the devices, and serialized the result. The next request repeated much of that work, even when few readings had changed. The proposed design stores each device as a hash of independently encoded metrics. An update replaces one field; a selective read decodes only the fields it needs. Assembled JSON has a separate place in the design: a short-lived local snapshot. Snapshot reuse and permission to query history are separate choices. Readers still need the age of each observation to judge how current that view is. 1 A slow view of current readings 2 The devices give us some room 3 Maintain what the table keeps asking for 4 Store metrics in the shape they arrive 4.1 Follow two metrics through the hash 5 Give updates a short window to meet 6 A fast lookup can still make a slow response 7 How fresh does this request need to be? 8 When the live state stops moving 9 Where the work belongs 10 References

sections.heading: 1 A slow view of current readings
sections.text: The table needed current readings from many devices. Behind it, the backend queried a time-series store for the most recent values of each metric, combined them into device-level structures, and returned the result. Work that was manageable for one device became expensive across a larger view. There was a reasonable explanation for every step. The observations lived in a time-series database, the table needed their latest values, and the backend assembled the response the client expected. Taken together, those steps made ordinary use painfully slow. The incoming data offers a smaller unit of work. Each observation changes one metric, while the table asks for an assembled view of many metrics. Keeping those two representations separate lets the update path stay small without making every reader reconstruct devices from history.

sections.heading: 2 The devices give us some room
sections.text: Consider physical meters, sensors, and controllers that report measurements periodically. A table of their latest observations does not necessarily need a reaction within milliseconds. The acceptable delay depends on what the view is used for. Each metric also arrives independently. A temperature observation may be newer than the last consumption reading. There is no single message containing the complete, current device. The table therefore needs the latest known observation for each metric. Those observations may have different ages. Keeping their timestamps matters: a newly assembled response must not make an old reading look newly measured. This leaves room to maintain the device's state between requests, and to reuse an assembled response briefly when the caller allows it.

sections.heading: 3 Maintain what the table keeps asking for
sections.text: The design adds a current-state projection alongside historical storage. As telemetry arrives, a consumer updates the latest metric values in a shared cache. The time-series store remains the historical source; the projection serves the recurring current-state lookup. For each device and metric, the merge rule is small: The per-metric merge rule, shown as pseudocode. if no value is stored, or incoming.timestamp > stored.timestamp: store incoming value and timestamp Under that rule, an older observation arriving late cannot replace a newer stored one. Different metrics can advance independently, so an out-of-order temperature update need not prevent a consumption update from being applied. The comparison and replacement need to happen atomically. Reading a timestamp and writing the value in separate operations would let concurrent updates overwrite one another. The timestamp must also be a meaningful ordering key; the rule cannot correct a wrongly timestamped observation. Figure 1: Conceptual update and read paths. The service can reuse local snapshots or load shared metric state. Historical queries for missing devices are separately controlled; a snapshot-only request uses neither backend. Historical ingestion is omitted. The state is an aggregate of observations, not a measurement of the whole device at one instant. That fits the table's purpose without pretending the devices report more synchronously than they do.

sections.heading: 4 Store metrics in the shape they arrive
sections.text: One option is a serialized JSON object for each device. That resembles the response, but changing a single metric means rewriting the object. Reading a subset also means deserializing unrelated values. The proposed layout uses one hash per device, with independently addressable metric fields [1]. Each field holds a compact byte string containing its timestamp, value, and optional unit. The cache selects the field; the application decodes what is inside it. Figure 2: One device hash maps metric names to individual byte strings. The expanded field shows fixed-width timestamp and length fields followed by variable-length UTF-8 contents. The illustrative temperature payload occupies 18 bytes; cell widths are schematic, and hash keys and storage overhead are excluded. Both text fields use the same decoding rule: read the length, then consume that many bytes. A missing unit has length zero and needs no separate parsing path. Although the decoder could infer the unit's length from the remaining buffer, the explicit length keeps it independent of that outer boundary and makes each metric payload self-delimiting, at a cost of one byte per metric. Values remain text in this representation; interpreting a reading as a number or another type is the reader's job. The fixed fields occupy 11 bytes: 8 for the timestamp in Unix milliseconds, 2 for the value's byte length, and 1 for the unit's byte length. The payload then needs as many bytes as the UTF-8 value and unit contain. In the example, the value 21.4 takes 4 bytes and the unit °C takes 3, giving 18 bytes (144 bits) in total. That counts the metric payload, not the field name, device key, or storage engine's overhead. A new voltage reading can then update voltage without reconstructing temperature and consumption. The service can also ask for the fields a particular view needs. Those selected fields still need decoding, but the others can remain untouched. The JSON response becomes something built from that state, rather than the unit that every update must replace.

sections.heading: 4.1 Follow two metrics through the hash
sections.text: Consider an initially empty hash for a fictional device. The timestamps below are ordered t0 < t1 < t2 < t3; arrival order differs from observation order.  Arrival Metric Timestamp Reading Effect First temperature t1 21.4 °C Store the temperature field Next voltage t2 3.5 V Store voltage; leave temperature at t1 Late temperature t0 20.9 °C Ignore it; the stored temperature is newer Latest temperature t3 21.8 °C Replace temperature; leave voltage at t2 A temperature-only read now selects that field and decodes 21.8 °C with timestamp t3. It does not fetch or decode voltage. A view needing both metrics can select both, retaining their different timestamps. Neither read needs to replay the arrivals to discover which values survived. This example describes the storage layout's capabilities. A public API can choose a coarser boundary, such as returning all metrics for the selected devices; field-level storage does not require field selection in every endpoint.

sections.heading: 5 Give updates a short window to meet
sections.text: Field-level updates remove the full-object rewrite. Issuing a separate request for every incoming metric would still create substantial network overhead under load. The consumer can briefly collect updates for each device, merge them, and write them together. The window should be small relative to the delay the application can accept. If the same metric appears more than once in the window, the newest timestamp wins there too. The stored state still needs its own atomic comparison when the batch is applied. There is no need to wait for unrelated devices. One device's updates can be flushed while another device's window is still open. The small delay buys fewer network round trips, which is a useful trade for readings that normally arrive seconds or minutes apart.

sections.heading: 6 A fast lookup can still make a slow response
sections.text: Once the state is cheap to read, the table still needs a response containing many devices. Fetching fields from the cache does not remove the CPU work of turning them into JSON. For repeated reads of one device, a short-lived JSON snapshot local to the read service can avoid rebuilding the same response. A request spanning many devices also needs efficient assembly: collect the selected fields into a shared buffer, reuse memory where practical, and reuse per-device snapshots when they fit the request. This gives the two cache representations different jobs. Metric fields are convenient to update and select. Serialized snapshots are convenient to return. Using both avoids making every update pay for a response that nobody may read, or making every reader assemble a response that was just assembled.

sections.heading: 7 How fresh does this request need to be?
sections.text: A routine table read can reuse unexpired local snapshots and load the devices missing from them. Those snapshots expire after a configured lifetime. If a reader wants a newly assembled response, it can skip existing snapshots and replace them with the loaded result. Another request can skip snapshot reads and writes altogether, leaving the local cache undisturbed. A snapshot-only read makes a different trade-off: it returns what is available locally without contacting either backend. That can mean a partial result, or an empty one when none of the requested devices are available. It does not start rebuilding the missing snapshots. Permission to query history is a separate choice. A table refresh can still read shared metric state while avoiding the cost of historical queries for missing devices. An existing snapshot may contain data obtained by an earlier historical lookup; disabling that lookup for this request does not change where an already cached result came from. There are two ages here. Snapshot age describes when the response was assembled. Observation age describes when the device produced a reading. A snapshot built now may contain a consumption value from several minutes ago. Expiring the snapshot does not make that measurement newer, and an old metric timestamp does not by itself trigger a historical query. The caller must judge the reading's age separately from the lifetime of its JSON representation. For a view that can accept a short delay, snapshot reuse avoids repeated assembly between device reports. A view of both metrics might reuse a device snapshot made before t3 while that snapshot remains unexpired. Skipping it would load the current metric state instead. Whether missing devices also trigger historical queries depends on the separate lookup policy.

sections.heading: 8 When the live state stops moving
sections.text: When a requested device is missing from shared metric state, the service can query history if the request allows it. The assembled result can enter the local snapshot cache when the snapshot policy permits. A request restricted to local snapshots never reaches this path. Without historical lookups, missing devices are omitted from the result. A failure to reach the shared cache is still an error, not proof that the devices have no readings. Keeping those cases separate prevents a backend outage from looking like a successful but empty table. If the consumer stops, cached readings stop advancing. Catching up requires retained events or reconstruction from history, including updates that were buffered but not written before the consumer exited. The merge rule still applies during recovery: a delayed rebuild must not replace a newer value already received from the stream. Observation timestamps help readers judge the result's age, but the service also needs to distinguish a quiet device from an ingestion path that has stopped receiving updates.

sections.heading: 9 Where the work belongs
sections.text: Historical storage remains useful for history and recovery. The proposed read path serves the usual request from maintained metric state, with short-lived local snapshots avoiding repeated assembly. Readers can control snapshot reuse without automatically enabling expensive historical lookups. The changes follow the work that was being repeated. Per-metric state avoids reconstructing devices from history. Short, per-device batches reduce write overhead. Response snapshots avoid assembling the same JSON for every reader. This is a useful pattern for periodic telemetry because the reporting intervals leave room for those trade-offs. Its suitability comes from what the screen needs to show, how observations arrive, and how much delay the caller can accept. Those decisions can be considered independently of the database products.

sections.heading: 10 References
sections.text: Redis, Redis hashes, a public example of field-addressable storage, not a statement of the deployed technology.

sections.text: Keeping Go services understandable and testable, so another engineer can change them safely and review work delegated to a coding agent. When someone needs to change a service I’ve worked on, I want them to be able to find the relevant behavior and test their change locally. That includes me after a few months away. The service should give us enough context to understand its dependencies and the boundaries a change needs to preserve. Hexagonal architecture gives me useful places to put those boundaries. Small interfaces keep the dependencies understandable. A common handler shape makes recurring work composable. Tests and architecture checks help keep those decisions in place as the service changes. That structure matters when I delegate a change, too. A coding agent can work from the booking contract and the checks around it. I want its result to come with evidence I can inspect, and its unanswered business questions to remain visible. Extract a booking operation both callers can use Let the application define its dependencies Use a common contract for application handlers Pass time into the booking rule Add logging and metrics with decorators Connect both adapters in the composition root Choose tests that exercise the failure you care about Decide when a booking can be retried Check architectural boundaries in the build Prepare the context for an agent's change Review the change and the evidence The full presentation References The handler and decorator approach owes a good deal to Three Dots Labs' Wild Workouts example. I've adapted the ideas to the services I work on. The delivery-booking example below uses neutral vocabulary to explain the structure; its booking rules are illustrative. I'll assume you can read Go functions and interfaces. We'll follow a booking operation from an HTTP endpoint into a shared application handler, then consider how to delegate that extraction to a coding agent. Along the way, the booking's expiry rule gives us a few decisions that the package structure cannot settle.

sections.heading: Extract a booking operation both callers can use
sections.text: Suppose an HTTP endpoint accepts a delivery booking. It decodes the request, checks whether a reservation hold is still valid, and writes a database document. All of that can fit in one handler. Then a broker consumer needs to accept bookings too. I want both entry points to use the same booking behavior. Copying the validation into the consumer would give me two places to update the next time the rule changes. Calling the HTTP endpoint from the consumer would make an internal operation depend on transport details it does not need. That gives the first extraction a specific purpose: move booking orchestration behind a callable application boundary. The HTTP endpoint keeps decoding requests and mapping results to responses. The broker consumer gets its own translation and delivery policy. Both call the booking operation. Before moving the code, I write down what the existing endpoint actually does. What counts as an expired hold? Which failure does the caller see when storage is unavailable? What happens if the same booking arrives again? If the answers are unclear, moving code is premature. A cleaner package layout would leave the uncertainty intact. I also establish a dependency check early: application code may not import a database adapter. Otherwise the extracted handler can grow a direct MongoDB dependency during the next change. The check gives the person making that change feedback about the boundary before it becomes a review comment. An existing service may not follow boundaries that I am only now introducing. I use a baseline to record the accepted findings, refuse new ones, and remove entries as their violations are fixed. That lets us preserve the new boundary without making every change depend on a service-wide rewrite. The identity of each finding matters. Keeping the total number unchanged would still allow a new violation to replace an old one. For example, these are two different findings under the same dependency rule: Illustrative finding labels for an application package importing its database adapter. existing: app/command/legacy.go -> adapters/mongodb new: app/command/book_delivery.go -> adapters/mongodb Fixing the import in legacy.go while adding it in book_delivery.go leaves the count at one. The new finding must still fail the check. Once the old finding is fixed, I remove it from the baseline so that restoring the forbidden import fails too. Figure 1: A dependency check rejects new violations while a baseline records the existing ones for gradual removal. Slide from the accompanying presentation.

sections.heading: Let the application define its dependencies
sections.text: For the booking operation, the application needs to record a delivery booking. It does not need to construct a BSON filter or know which MongoDB collection stores it. A driven port declared in the application package that consumes it. type DeliveryBookingRepository interface { RecordDeliveryBooking( context.Context, booking.DeliveryBooking, ) error } I declare this interface beside the booking handler. The database adapter implements it using domain values at the boundary and its own persistence representation internally. Go's implicit interface implementation lets the concrete adapter satisfy the interface without importing the application package merely to declare that relationship. The Go code review guidance recommends placing interfaces with their consumers. This is a driven port: something the application calls. The operation the HTTP adapter invokes is a driving port: a way to ask the application to do work. Both contracts belong to the application core. Cockburn's original Ports and Adapters description makes this ability to drive the application independently of its eventual UI and database central to the design. The distinction between dependencies and calls takes a moment to get used to. At runtime, the booking handler calls the database adapter through an interface. In source code, the application refers to its own interface, while the adapter refers to domain types and provides the required method. The application has no import of the adapter. Figure 2: Both contracts belong to the core. The use case depends on its driven port, and the database adapter implements that contract; these arrows describe code dependencies, not the direction of every runtime call. A small arrangement might look like this: One possible layout. The interfaces live with application code; the composition root connects their implementations. internal/ booking/ domain/ booking values and rules app/command/ BookDelivery and its repository port app/query/ read operations adapters/http/ request and response translation adapters/mongodb/ persistence mapping service/ construction, wiring, and lifecycle There is no need to create all of these packages before they contain useful work. The import direction is what I preserve when I introduce a boundary. I also avoid creating a general repository interface simply because the MongoDB implementation has several methods. That would make each caller depend on the provider's entire API. The booking handler asks for the behavior it needs. Another use case can have a different interface, even if one concrete adapter satisfies both. Small does not have to mean one method. If a consumer needs a coherent set of operations with shared transaction semantics, splitting it into several unrelated interfaces can obscure that requirement. The consumer's contract determines the boundary. HTTP structs can carry JSON tags, MongoDB documents can carry BSON tags, and the domain keeps its own values. This costs mapping code. I accept that cost when it prevents storage or transport changes from spreading into business rules, and I test the mappings because they can be wrong too. For a small service whose work consists almost entirely of storing and returning records, I may keep a concrete implementation and a few functions for longer. Here, the second caller gives the booking boundary a job: keep the hold rule shared while each adapter handles its own protocol. I introduce the extra structure when I can explain what change or test it makes easier.

sections.heading: Use a common contract for application handlers
Pass time into the booking rule
Add logging and metrics with decorators
Connect both adapters in the composition root
sections.text:
With the operation constructed, the composition root supplies it to both adapters: Illustrative adapter constructors accept the same typed booking handler. HTTP registration and the broker consumer loop are omitted. httpAdapter := bookinghttp.New(bookDelivery)
brokerAdapter := bookingbroker.New(bookDelivery)
 Each adapter constructor accepts decorator.Handler[command.BookDelivery, decorator.Void]. The HTTP adapter translates its decoded request into command.BookDelivery; the broker adapter translates a booking event into that same command. The repository and clock are already supplied to the shared handler, so the adapters do not need them. That reuse depends on both callers needing the same booking behavior. Concurrent calls also require the repository, clock and decorators to support overlapping invocations. Request-specific values stay inside each Handle call; a metrics wrapper that shares a mutable counter across calls must synchronize its updates. Consider an in-process test with a fixed clock and a recording repository. Through each adapter, submit a booking whose hold has expired. Both should reject it without a repository call. With a fresh repository for each path, submit a valid booking and check the recorded ID and deadline. That scenario exercises both translations and the shared rule. The adapters can still map the rejection differently: an HTTP response and a broker processing outcome serve different callers. Adding the broker path now requires its event mapping and consumer wiring. The domain rule and MongoDB mapping stay where they were. For the existing HTTP endpoint, I also keep tests that check its response contract. Calling the new handler successfully would leave that part unchecked. The composition root also creates the database clients and other long-lived resources, passes them to adapters, and coordinates shutdown. A handler does not create a fresh client for every call. Workers need cancellation and a way to finish or abandon in-flight work before their dependencies close. A common Handle method can serve a worker's application operation; scheduling and recovery remain part of the worker's design.

sections.heading: Choose tests that exercise the failure you care about
Decide when a booking can be retried
sections.text:
A broker consumer adds another reason to distinguish a handler result from its delivery contract. Consider this sequence: An external side effect and a broker offset commit can be separated by a crash. Receive booking -> record booking -> crash -> commit offset never happens
                                   |
                                   +-> recovery may deliver the booking again
 The application can return an error or a successful result. The surrounding consumer loop decides how that result affects retries and offset commits. A callback returning nil is not itself a broker acknowledgement. Recovery depends on how processing and offset persistence are coordinated. Dropping malformed input, quarantining it, and retrying it indefinitely are different operational policies. A permanent booking rejection is also different from losing the connection to storage. I want the adapter's error mapping to state which outcome it chooses, with tests that exercise the consumer loop where necessary. A database write can succeed while its acknowledgement is lost. The caller cannot tell whether another attempt will create a duplicate. The expiry rule makes the ambiguity more apparent: a first attempt might succeed before the deadline, then a retry after the deadline fails in the domain constructor before reaching storage. Suppose we decide that an identical retry of an accepted booking should return the recorded success, even after the hold expires. A request using that identity with different input should fail as a conflict. A genuinely new booking must still pass the expiry check. This is one possible extension to the example's business contract. The handler shown above does not implement that extension. It would need to recognize prior acceptance before applying first-attempt validation again. The persistence contract would also need to distinguish an identical repeat from a conflicting request and coordinate competing submissions atomically. An unprotected lookup followed by an insert would leave a race between callers. A stable ID by itself does not specify any of these outcomes. I need to agree on those semantics with the people who own booking behavior, then test them against the repository implementation. The signature of RecordDeliveryBooking says little about duplicates or concurrent calls. Until the contract is agreed and implemented, I keep automatic retries disabled. The extraction should preserve existing behavior; changing its repeat semantics deserves a separate decision and tests. Once the operation is safe to repeat under the agreed conditions, the consumer can retry eligible failures with a bounded policy. If recording the booking must also publish an event atomically from the application's perspective, that creates another consistency problem to design for, often with an outbox or another explicit coordination mechanism. My backpressure article makes a related distinction between a required event path and a best-effort cache update. An optional projection can sometimes discard work. A booking acceptance path needs its own answer about which work may be lost and which must survive recovery.

sections.heading: Check architectural boundaries in the build
sections.text:
Once the booking handler exists, I want a build to tell me when application code imports MongoDB directly. Otherwise I am relying on every reviewer remembering the original extraction. A service-specific analyzer can use Go's analysis API to inspect package imports, struct tags, and selected calls. In my arrangement, the domain cannot import application or adapter packages, declare serialization tags, or call time.Now. Application code cannot import concrete adapters. The composition root is where those implementations meet. The details of the check matter. An import alias must not hide a forbidden dependency. Checking a call's resolved object is stronger than searching source text for the spelling time.Now(). I also need to decide which files the rule covers: production code, generated code, and test harnesses have different roles. Those choices should be visible in the analyzer and its tests. A build target can run a project-specific analyzer through go vet: An illustrative Make target. The service supplies its own archvet tool and rule tests. lint-architecture:
	mkdir -p .bin
	go build -o .bin/archvet ./tools/archvet
	go vet -vettool=$(CURDIR)/.bin/archvet ./internal/...
 I test the analyzer against deliberately invalid packages and examples that should remain valid. A changed package path or a rule that reports every harmless import can make a check ineffective just as easily as a missing rule can. This is the part of evolutionary architecture I find practical: identify a property worth preserving and give it repeatable feedback as the system changes. An import rule covers a particular dependency decision. It cannot determine whether RecordDeliveryBooking represents the right business operation, whether the fake models its contract correctly, or whether the delivery policy is acceptable. I still want the diagram, too. Generating a component diagram from the composed application avoids maintaining a second handwritten inventory of its wiring. After changing the composition, I regenerate it and review the diff. Its scope depends on what the generator discovers; an object graph does not explain every dynamic runtime interaction.

sections.heading: Prepare the context for an agent's change
sections.text: I can now describe a bounded task to a coding agent: Extract booking orchestration from the HTTP endpoint into an application handler that another adapter can call. Preserve the existing HTTP behavior and hold-expiry rule. Keep database details in the adapter. Report any unclear repeat behavior before changing it. The agent still needs to find the current endpoint and its tests, follow its persistence dependency, and inspect the composition that connects them. The architecture check and its baseline explain which dependencies the change must preserve. A similar handler elsewhere in the repository can help with the extraction, provided its business policy is not copied along with its structure. I use agentic enrichment to mean gathering relevant repository knowledge around a change. For the booking extraction, that means following the endpoint to its dependencies and finding the test that states what happens at expiry. The agent can read the import rule when deciding where to put the extracted code. Selecting and retrieving information as work progresses is also part of the context-engineering approach described by Anthropic. A context note for this extraction might read: The domain constructor rejects a hold at its deadline. Keep that decision in booking.NewDeliveryBooking. The application handler should supply the time value and call the repository port. Preserve the HTTP adapter's error mapping. Identical retries after expiry remain an open policy decision. In the repository, I would attach the inspected revision and links to the constructor and the existing HTTP test. The agent then has a reason to preserve the clock input as it moves the orchestration, and a specific policy question to leave open during the extraction. I want to know where the agent's conclusions came from. Tooling can inspect an import, while a decision record may explain why that dependency was forbidden. A test gives evidence about the scenario it exercises. If the agent suggests that repeated bookings should be harmless, it has proposed a policy. Before that becomes implementation, I need agreement from the people responsible for booking behavior. If a port or its callers change, an earlier summary may no longer describe the operation. I want the context to identify the repository revision and point to the relevant files and checks, so the agent can inspect them again when the code changes. A generated dependency graph helps locate code; its arrows cannot explain the meaning of an accepted booking. In my experimental JAMES project, an architecture profile describes roles and their path bindings, along with conventions such as port ownership and decorator order. The profile helps an agent relate an application handler to its place in the repository. A declared rule only becomes enforced when a supported validator executes it and the workflow uses its result. You can start with repository instructions and existing build targets; a separate orchestration tool is optional.

sections.heading: Review the change and the evidence
sections.text: For the booking extraction, I first ask the agent to identify the behavior already covered and the cases the change could disturb. Before moving code, I temporarily let an expired hold through and confirm that the relevant test fails. I restore the implementation before continuing with the extraction. That tells me the test detects this particular mistake; other faults still need their own checks. During the move, suppose the agent puts a MongoDB call in the application handler. The import analyzer should reject it. The agent can repair the dependency by putting the contract beside its consumer and leaving the concrete adapter outside. That repair still needs the behavior tests: correct imports would allow an implementation that quietly discards a storage error. For a move confined to orchestration, I start with the booking rule and handler tests. Changed mappings need adapter tests too. If the diff touches wiring or startup, I include the corresponding composition or built-service checks. The test scopes described earlier help me choose which parts must run for real. The agent's report should let a reviewer follow a claim to the check that supports it. If it says HTTP behavior is unchanged, I want the relevant scenario and result. Commands and their results belong with that report, including anything that could not run. I also want the gaps stated plainly: a function-fake test gives me no evidence about a MongoDB index or a consumer's offset handling. Tests and rules can need changes too, and I review those changes explicitly. A failing check should send the agent back to investigate; deleting an assertion or broadening the baseline needs a justification of its own. When the same agent writes the implementation and its tests, they can share the same mistaken interpretation. I compare the change with existing characterization tests and the agreed requirement, and keep the analyzer's own fixtures under test. Figure 5: Characterize the behavior, move orchestration behind the port, verify the new wiring, then remove resolved baseline entries. Review still decides whether the boundary makes sense. The extraction is finished when the protected booking behavior still holds, the consumer owns its repository contract, the application no longer imports its adapter, and the wiring is checked at an appropriate scope. Any resolved baseline entries leave with the change. For the next caller, I can concentrate on its request mapping and delivery behavior. The booking operation remains shared. If that caller needs a different answer to the retry-after-expiry question, we can discuss the affected application and persistence contracts before changing them.
